articles.title: How people in Montenegro are making their country cleaner
articles.author: Daria Dergacheva
paras: And helping to make the goals for EU accession plausible
Originally published on Global Voices
Screenshot from the EkoMapa website of the EkoGard organization in Montenegro. Fair use.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

Montenegro is on its way to joining the EU; at the moment, the goal is to do so by 2028. The United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE) review in 2025 states that the country has made significant progress in aligning its environmental legal and regulatory framework, as well as much of its national legislation, with European Union (EU) directives.
However, some problems remain, including waste management and a very low recycling rate — less than 2 percent, far below the EU’s 50 percent target.

Austrian Member of Parliament Thomas Waitz (Greens/EFA), chair of the delegation to the EU-Montenegro Stabilisation and Association Parliamentary Committee, said in an interview with The New Union Post that there have been “massive improvements” in Montenegro, citing as an example the closure of more than 100 illegal landfills in the last year: “It is a great effort for such a small country. But they have another 500, and if we expected them to have them all cleaned up, it would be impossible.”

While politicians and international agencies discuss how Montenegro could get closer to the target and put its waste management under control, ordinary citizens are making practical steps to improve the situation today.
This Digital Spark spotlight story is about one such organization, EkoGard, and the many people who participate in its efforts and, step by step, try to make Montenegro cleaner.
Global Voices interviewed the organization’s founder and general director, Senad Pepić, about the impact of Digital Spark and its community initiative.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project.

Senad Pepić (SP): EkoGard was built through years of work on the ground, not in an office. It grew out of the Očistimo Rožaje initiative, where we spent six years building a strong community of people ready to take action. We started with illegal dumpsites, but our work gradually expanded to other environmental and social issues affecting everyday life. We organized cleanups, worked with young people, launched campaigns, and encouraged residents to tackle problems that kept coming back. We joined Digital Spark because we wanted to bring what we learned in the field together with digital tools and data. We hoped to show a fuller picture of the problems and change how people talk about them. EkoMapa grew out of that idea as a natural next step in our work.
GV: What issue or challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

SP: One cleanup in particular made us rethink our approach. We cleared an illegal dumpsite beside a rural road, in an area where residents had no suitable place to dispose of their waste. The nearest legal disposal point was about six kilometers away. After the cleanup, we asked for a waste container to be installed and were promised that the problem would be addressed. Three years passed; the container was never installed, and the dumpsite returned. Its return changed how we saw similar sites elsewhere. We had photos, posts, and letters from other areas, but no way to see the full extent of the problem or how it related to gaps in waste collection services. We wanted to map these places and understand the conditions in each settlement. Doing that gives us a way to show local institutions where waste disposal services are lacking and talk about what needs to change.
GV: What are the key changes or activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

SP: Before this project, EkoGard organized cleanups, worked with young people, held educational activities, ran campaigns, and drew attention to local problems. Through Digital Spark, we began collecting and analysing what we saw in the field more systematically. EkoMapa started as a map of illegal dumpsites, but it grew into a tool for understanding environmental conditions across the community. We decided to look at conditions settlement by settlement, so we could connect the problems we found with the services available to residents. We also developed a model that uses the information we collect to assess environmental risks and gaps in local services in each settlement. It helps us spot patterns, compare needs across settlements, and discuss what the data shows with local institutions.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

SP: Our activists now have a practical tool and a clearer way to document what they find. We can use that information in public campaigns and make a stronger case for change. For residents, we can now show how the problems they face relate to the services available in their settlements. Organizations from other towns and countries have also shown interest in using the tool to understand conditions in their own communities and involve residents in finding solutions. The local waste management company has also recognized that the information could be useful in its work. For now, the clearest changes are in how our activists work and in the conversations we have begun with other organizations and local institutions. Changes on the ground will take longer.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?

SP: Through the project, we learned that giving people a way to report a problem is only a first step. They also need to know why we collect the information, what we will do with it, and how it might lead to change. The training on how to reach people and communicate more clearly was especially useful. It made us think about the words we use and how to talk about problems without making people feel powerless. For us, digital democracy means residents can help identify problems and take part in finding solutions. When we collect, check, and present what they tell us clearly, it can inform our campaigns and conversations with institutions. It also helps us ask for clearer answers.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

SP: The most valuable lesson is that technology cannot solve a problem on its own. It can help us see what is happening across a community, but it cannot replace fieldwork, talking with residents, or working with institutions. Finding a problem on a map is just the beginning. We also need to understand why it happened. If we only deal with what we can see, the same problem is likely to return. When we bring the data together with people’s experiences, we can start to propose solutions that meet their needs. That is what we will take into our future work: listen, look for patterns and causes, and use what we learn to push for change.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

SP: Our next step is to present our findings to the local government and make the case for better planning of waste collection and other local services. We want to draw attention to settlements that have been overlooked for years and follow up on how institutions respond. We are already applying what we learned to EkoGard’s wider work, especially our campaigns and how we involve residents. Together with other organizations from Montenegro, we are preparing a campaign to establish a National Eco Line, a nationwide channel for reporting environmental problems and following up on how the responsible authorities respond. We know the results may take time, so we will keep working with other organizations and local institutions.

articles.title: Big Tech, AI, and the quiet expansion of digital surveillance in Nigeria
articles.author: Nshua Cali-Dibang
paras: How much control do people retain over their personal information in a world increasingly shaped by AI?
Originally published on Global Voices
Illustration by Nshua Cali-Dibang, used with permission.

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Every search, social media interaction, and conversation with an artificial intelligence (AI) tool can leave behind information about its user. Individually, these digital traces may appear insignificant. Collectively, however, they can reveal interests, habits, preferences and patterns of behavior that have considerable commercial and political value.

As AI becomes increasingly embedded in everyday life, technology companies are finding new ways to use data to develop their products, personalize services and generate revenue. While these developments offer considerable benefits, they also raise a difficult question: How much control do people retain over their personal information in a world increasingly shaped by AI?

The issue extends beyond privacy policies and user agreements. It concerns the growing power of technology companies to collect information, draw conclusions about individuals, and influence the digital environments in which people communicate, work, and access information.
The business of knowing more about us

In September 2024, the United States Federal Trade Commission (FTC) published findings from an investigation into nine major social media and video-streaming companies, including Meta, YouTube, TikTok, and Amazon-owned Twitch.

The FTC reported that these companies collected extensive information about users and, in some cases, non-users. The information included personal details, interests, online activities, and data obtained from other sources. The investigation also raised concerns about lengthy data retention, inadequate privacy protections, and the use of personal information in automated systems, including AI.

The report highlighted a fundamental imbalance: Companies can accumulate substantial information about individuals, while those individuals may have limited understanding of how their data is used or how to prevent certain uses.

AI adds another dimension to this problem. Data can help train models, improve recommendations, and power automated decisions. However, the greater the volume and variety of information companies can access, the more important it becomes to establish clear limits on its collection and use.

The concern is not that every company collecting data is necessarily acting maliciously. Rather, it is that systems designed to maximize commercial value from information can create incentives to collect more data than people reasonably expect or understand.

For millions of people, AI offers opportunities that were previously difficult to access. Students can use AI tools to support learning, small businesses can improve their operations, and journalists can explore new approaches to research and production.

In countries such as Nigeria, where access to resources and professional services can be uneven, these tools could help narrow certain gaps. AI systems that support local languages and reflect diverse cultural experiences could also make digital services more accessible.

Yet inclusion should mean more than allowing people to use a technology. It should also mean ensuring that they understand the conditions under which they use it and retain meaningful rights over their information.

Many digital services are governed by lengthy terms and privacy policies that users may accept without fully understanding the implications. Some AI products also raise questions about whether information submitted through prompts, uploaded documents, or other interactions may be retained or used to improve models.

The precise practices differ between companies and products. Nevertheless, users need clear explanations of what information is collected, why it is needed, how long it is retained, and whether it may be used for purposes beyond the immediate service.
Without these safeguards, the benefits of AI inclusion risk coming with an invisible cost: reduced control over personal information.
When corporate power begins to resemble surveillance

The connection between big tech and authoritarianism requires careful examination. Authoritarianism is not simply the collection of data by private companies. It involves the concentration and exercise of power in ways that undermine accountability, rights, and freedoms.

However, extensive corporate data collection can create conditions that make surveillance easier. Detailed personal information can support profiling, targeted persuasion and the prediction of individual behavior. Depending on the circumstances, businesses, governments, or other actors may exploit these capabilities.

The risks become particularly serious when personal data can be accessed or shared without adequate safeguards, when automated systems make consequential decisions without meaningful oversight, or when people have little opportunity to challenge how their information is used.

Concentrated corporate power adds another concern. When a small number of companies control widely used digital platforms, AI services, and large pools of information, individuals may have few practical alternatives. Leaving a platform may mean losing access to professional networks, customers, communities, or essential services.

This does not mean that every AI system is a surveillance tool or that every technology company intends to restrict freedom. It means that the infrastructure of digital life deserves scrutiny because its capabilities can be used in ways that extend beyond their original commercial purpose.
Nigeria’s data protection challenge

Nigeria has a legal framework intended to protect individuals against the misuse of their personal information. The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 established the Nigeria Data Protection Commission and provides a framework for the lawful, fair and accountable processing of personal data.
Legislation is an important step, but effective protection also depends on implementation, public awareness, and regulators’ ability to hold organizations accountable.

As Nigerians increasingly adopt AI-powered services, questions about data governance become more pressing. Users need to understand their rights, while organizations must take responsibility for explaining their practices and protecting the information they collect.

There is also a wider question of representation. If AI systems are developed using data that inadequately reflects Nigerian languages, cultures, and social realities, their benefits may be distributed unevenly. Responsible AI governance must therefore address both the protection of personal information and the inclusion of communities whose experiences are often underrepresented.

UNESCO’s Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence emphasizes privacy, data protection, transparency, accountability, and fairness throughout the AI lifecycle. These principles provide a useful foundation for ensuring that technological progress respects human rights.
Innovation must not come at the expense of control

The challenge is not to reject AI or prevent companies from using data to develop useful technologies. It is to establish boundaries that allow innovation without making personal privacy an acceptable casualty.

Technology companies should minimize unnecessary data collection, communicate their policies clearly, provide meaningful choices, and strengthen protections against unauthorized access. Regulators must ensure that existing laws remain effective as AI capabilities evolve, while users need accessible information about the rights available to them.

Ultimately, digital inclusion cannot be measured solely by the number of people using AI. It must also consider whether those people can participate safely, understand the systems they rely on, and exercise meaningful control over their information.

As AI becomes more powerful, the question is no longer simply what technology can do with our data. It is who decides what can be done, who benefits from those decisions, and who has the power to challenge them.
The future of AI should not be defined only by what machines learn about us, but also by how much control we retain over ourselves.

articles.title: Venezuela welcomes opposition leader María Corina Machado home
articles.author: Óscar Calles
paras: Machado returns to a hopeful, cautious nation
Originally published on Global Voices
María Corina Machado arriving in Caracas after months of hiding and exile. Photo by Óscar Calles, 2026. Used with permission.

Thousands of people took to the Valle-Coche highway in Caracas to welcome the opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate María Corina Machado, who returned to Venezuela after 16 months in hiding and ten months in exile. The massive gathering was one of celebration, but her compatriots were also filled with doubts about what comes next.

After more than a year in the shadows, forced into hiding following her kidnapping — allegedly by government paramilitaries — at her last public protest in 2025, Machado quietly slipped out of the country. She emerged on the global stage later that year to receive the Nobel Peace Prize honoring her social organization campaign during Venezuela’s 2024 presidential elections, which were ultimately stolen by Nicolás Maduro. Since the former Venezuelan president’s capture on January 3, 2026, Machado has tried — and failed — to enter the country on at least seven occasions, claiming that the administration established by U.S. President Donald Trump didn’t allow her in.

On the morning of October 25, however, Machado was spotted in the city of Barquisimeto, where she visited the Santa Rosa church, and at about 10:25 that evening, her caravan passed through Santa Mónica, along the main route that leads to Venezuela’s captital:
Estoy aquí. Con ustedes — María Corina Machado (@MariaCorinaYA) October 25, 2026

Drivers excitedly honked their horns; in a crowd of about 3,000, people shouted slogans. Starting from the state of Lara, Machado’s caravan crossed Yaracuy, Carabobo, and Aragua as it inched toward Caracas — a journey of more than 300 kilometres that took her nearly 11 hours to complete.

On the heels of the January 3 United States military operation that captured Nicolás Maduro, whose 2024 re-election was questioned both inside and outside of Venezuela, then vice president Delcy Rodríguez took over as interim president.

Since August, her interim government has been negotiating with Dinorah Figuera, president of the National Assembly who was elected in 2015, in a Washington-driven dialogue process. Despite having promoted participation in the 2024 presidential elections, Machado’s party, Vente Venezuela, has had no representation in those negotiations.
The crowd waited for hours for Maria Corina Machado's arrival to the capital city. Photo by Óscar Calles, 2026. Used with permission.

Yet, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio attributed Machado’s safe return to those talks, which he claimed had already allowed for the release of hundreds of political prisoners and the return of hundreds of exiled opposition figures. Rubio called on all political actors to back them because they represent “the best opportunity Venezuela has had in thirty years.”

Faced with political demobilization, Venezuelans are used to seeing protests where the majority of participants are activists, leaders, and members of civil society organizations — people who are well-informed because it is their job to be — but Machado’s gathering was different. There were people without party shirts or hats; just a combination of families, friends, and civilians who seemed motivated by her return and hopeful for their country.

People began to assemble on the highway around 3:00 p.m. local time. After hours of waiting, the gathering turned into a party — the type of celebration that many did not dare to have after January 3.

Machado barely spoke; she did not have a megaphone and was in the tray of a pickup truck with a security detail around her. She gave no statements to the media during the caravan; instead, she listened to and greeted the crowd, hugging people, touching their hands, and letting herself be seen. On this occasion, people did not go to hear proposals, but simply to see her.

At one point, two patrols from the Directorate General of Military Counterintelligence (DGCIM) passed by. The people closest to the highway lane began shouting at them, “Get out, get out!” but no one blocked their path or touched their doors or windows and the patrols continued on their way. Known as Venezuela’s political police, the DGCIM was one of the bodies singled out for 2024’s repressive post-election measures, in which more than 2,300 people were detained.

Asked about the possible aftermaths of Machado’s return, caravan participants shared differing perspectives. Veterinarian Marianna Torres had no doubts about the order of things: Venezuela must have presidential elections, and soon, but not with the same electoral institutions that have permitted electoral fraud in the past. For her, all branches of power are corrupt and must be cleaned up before any election.

She also urged people looking at Venezuela from the outside to stop listening solely to politicians and pay attention to what “everyday Venezuelans” — the ones who know there are still political prisoners, human rights violations, and government authoritarian control — are saying.

Gabriela Santander, a publicist and activist for the Encuentro Ciudadano party, thought almost the opposite regarding the timeline. Stressing that she had been waiting for this day for months, since before Machado left, she believes that going to vote now, without an independent electoral arbiter or an impartial Supreme Tribunal of Justice (TSJ), would be falling into a trap. Her deadline is concrete: if a new Electoral National Center is not in place by the end of the first quarter of 2027, the time to put on pressure will arrive.

Santander suspects that behind Machado’s return — which she believes could not have happened without Washington's approval — are agreements that no one has disclosed, especially since Rubio confirmed that his government had negotiated her return with the interim government “many weeks ago.” What Santander noticed the night of the caravan, however, was something more important: people had been on the highway for more than four hours and authorities had not tried to detain them.

Attorney Joyffer Briceño took a pragmatic view of the situation. While he sees Machado as the leader of those who want to restore the country’s institutions, he does not mistake emotion for change. “Those who hold power today are the same ones who were part of the crisis for years,” he explained. “I want something less abstract than an economic growth figure; I want the improvement to be felt in the pockets of every Venezuelan.”

For José Gregorio Rodríguez Cham, Machado’s arrival carries a different weight. His father, Julio Rodríguez Salazar, is a political prisoner, so he attended the event with other relatives to continue demanding the release of the 322 political prisoners who, according to Foro Penal, remain detained. He believes that new elections would be different because of the oversight of the United States, but he does not deny that the repressive apparatus in Venezuela remains intact, and that dismantling it will take time. What he years for in the coming months are elections and freedom, starting with that of his family.
Photo by Óscar Calles, 2026. Used with permission.

Raquel Bugallo, a merchant in Caracas, remains somewhat suspicious of outside help. She believes that the international humanitarian aid Venezuela expected was overshadowed by economic interests, and that oil has been both Venezuela’s greatest wealth and “worst curse.” While she didn’t reject Rubio's call for understanding among all sectors, she did attach a condition: finding common ground, as long as the country can move forward. Her message to the international community was the shortest of the night: “If you are not going to help us, don’t get in our way.”

The day after Machado’s return, Delcy Rodríguez quipped that “the show could have been avoided.” Meanwhile, the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights reminded the Venezuelan state of its obligation to guarantee the life, integrity, and political rights of the leader. Between November 11 and 15, the dialogue table will meet again, for the first time with Machado inside the country.

In the meantime, Venezuelans can savour the feeling of having spent hours on the streets without that familiar fear of repression. While repressive bodies were still present, passing in patrols through the crowd, on October 25, 2026, with Machado waving from the back of a pickup truck, the people stared back at them and told them to go, which must have felt something like progress.

articles.title: Global Voices condemns the attacks on Albanian fact-checking service Faktoje
articles.author: Global Voices
paras: Faktoje is a respected member of the international fact-checking community
Originally published on Global Voices

Since October 27, at least 20 online media outlets and social media accounts in Albania have been waging a coordinated attack against the staff of fact-checking media service Faktoje Center, based in Tirana. A partner of Global Voices, Faktoje has been promoting accountability based on the right to information and transparency since 2018.

Faktoje and its team members, in particular its director, Klodiana Kapo, are facing a series of coordinated attacks from media outlets that have been circulating and reproducing articles that question Faktoje’s funding, financial management and independence, using its publicly available financial statements to cast doubt on the organisation’s credibility.

Faktoje is a certified signatory of the Code of Principles of the International Fact-Finding Network and the Code of Standards of the European Fact-Checking Standards Network. Both require high levels of public transparency in disclosing sources of funding and methodologies of work. This coordinated campaign aims to undermine the impact of Faktoje’s important work by maliciously using financial information that the organization voluntarily publishes, but stripping it of context and mischaracterizing its influence.

Faktoje considers these attacks to be directly connected to its fact-checking activities under its partnership with Meta, in the context of its recent fact-checking work covering the ongoing protests and debunking misleading narratives targeting protesters.

Since its inception eight years ago, Faktoje has stood at the forefront of the fight for freedom of expression, independent journalism, and information integrity in Albania and the wider Balkans region, including participation in the regional Western Balkans Anti-Disinformation Hub, the Anti-Disinformation Network for the Balkans and the continent-wide European Digital Media Observatory – EDMO Network.

Faktoje is a respected member of the international fact-checking community. Albanian authorities and European institutions need to speak up publicly for independent fact-checkers and journalists, and to ensure their safety, while media outlets reporting on civil society funding need to do so accurately and in context.

Global Voices joins the European Fact-Checking Standards Network and the International Fact-Checking Network in vehemently condemning those attacks on our partner. We stand in solidarity with our colleagues.

articles.title: We need to talk about Meta: Political interference and interests in the Brazilian elections
articles.author: R. Marie Santini, Professora da Escola de Comunicação e diretora do NetLab (Internet and Social Media Research Lab), Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ)
paras: On the eve of Donald Trump’s return to the presidency of the United States, in January 2025, Meta’s founder and CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, announced that changes would be made to his company’s moderation policies in the name of “freedom of expression”, which, he said, was under threat by global pressures for what he saw as censorship. The announcement signaled a rapprochement between Meta and the far right around a common goal: the deregulation of Big Tech. Since then, growing entanglement between major technology companies and the U.S. President Donald Trump administration has shown how the private interests of a small group can override the public interest.

In recent months, allegations have been mounting that Big Tech companies, especially Meta, have been interfering in the Brazilian electoral process this year, aiming to undermine the reelection of President Lula (PT). This kind of accusation is not new. Over the past decade, a vast body of literature has exposed the mediating role played by digital platforms in foreign interference in elections around the world. These reports have also highlight the challenges of holding companies accountable for allowing these interference campaigns to be amplified.

At our research group, NetLab UFRJ, we have spent years investigating how major digital platforms shape public debate and influence people’s perceptions of reality, often outside the regulatory and normative frameworks in force in Brazil. Meta in particular has become fertile ground for disinformation and boosting fraudulent ads, which already account for 10% of its annual revenue.

Despite lawsuits and administrative actions brought by Brazilian authorities against Meta, complaints and requests from civil society for investigations, as well as reports published by the press, the company has shown neither the willingness nor the diligence needed to effectively fight this kind of content.

Given this troubling track record, NetLab UFRJ created the “Big Tech Observatory” during the 2026 election campaign period in order to monitor how Meta and other digital platforms performed in two key areas: algorithmic recommendation and political advertising. The initiative set out to examine whether these companies would comply with the current Brazilian legislation established by the Electoral Supreme Court (TSE). The results of the analyses, however, told a predictable story.

We found that, between July and September, Meta received approximately R$ 2 million (US$ 400,000) for running 1,613 ads placed from outside Brazil that aimed to either favor or harm candidates. All were paid for in foreign currencies and boosted by pages with declared locations in other countries. The amount invested in this advertising is equivalent to that spent on prominent campaigns, including the race for Presidency and other executive offices.

Brazilian electoral law expressly prohibits candidates from receiving cash or donations in-kind from abroad. This ban, however, did not prevent the ads from being displayed to Brazilian users of Meta’s platforms. According to the available information, not only the ads were allowed to circulate but they may have reached up to 171 million views in the country.

But the irregularities in advertising do not stop there. Brazilian electoral rules prohibit electoral advertising from 48 hours before the polls to 24 hours afterwards. However, our analyses of both rounds of the 2026 election identified hundreds of ads in favor or against specific candidates that circulated on Meta’s platforms with no apparent restrictions. The company even allowed fake profiles posing as official channels of the Electoral Supreme Court to boost disinformation about a supposed “digital vote” which stated that people would be allowed to cast their vote from home on the day of the first round — something which does not exist in the Brazilian electoral system.

In addition to these irregularities, Lula’s political campaign page was temporarily disabled by Meta without explanation, preventing it from running electoral ads. On September 23, his Worker´s Party (PT) reported they had been blocked from advertising on Meta’s platforms. In a statement released on October 16, the company rejected the accusations of election interference and attributed the temporary deactivation to an “incorrect anti-fraud review” carried out under an agreement with the federal government to fight fraud involving public programs.

The effectiveness of the company’s anti-fraud measures, however, is questionable: an analysis carried out by NetLab UFRJ identified hundreds of fraudulent ads involving federal public policies circulating before and after September 23, indicating that those same measures were not able to stop this kind of content from running during the same period.

Finally, we found signs of discriminatory practices in ad pricing. Based on data released by Meta, we estimate that for the first round Lula’s campaign may have paid between 33% and 43% more than his far right adversary Flávio Bolsonaro campaign to reach the same number of users on Meta’s platforms. Despite this substantial difference, limitations in the company’s transparency policies make it impossible to identify precisely which parameters and criteria are used to price ads and, consequently, to draw definitive conclusions about the mechanisms behind this disparity. Even so, studies conducted in other contexts, such as the United States, India and the Netherlands, also point to evidence of discriminatory pricing practices in the platform’s advertising.

Other complaints made during the elections add to this overall scenario of negligence and show that, despite being worth billions and their strategic position at the forefront of technological innovation, major digital platforms invest little in protecting their users. For example, this 2026 election in Brazil saw several controversies involving WhatsApp’s image generation service, powered by the Meta AI artificial intelligence. Users reported being able to generate content favorable to Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign without difficulty, whereas they were not getting the same results for Lula. Meanwhile, the documentary channel Revelando had videos criticizing Flávio Bolsonaro removed from its Instagram profiles shortly after they were posted, without clear justification from the company.

These episodes cast doubt on the consistency of Meta’s moderation and content control systems, exposing failures that call for greater investment and improvement. The situation is made worse by the absence of transparent criteria or guarantees of equal treatment in how ads are handled, how content is recommended, how advertising is priced, and how profiles and posts are moderated.

Big Tech companies have developed predatory business models, and they are currently joining forces with political forces committed to deregulation in Brazil. This is part of a strategy to protect their businesses and expand their room for maneuver.

Whether or not one side of the electoral race is being deliberately favored, it is indisputable that the major digital platforms continuously exercise the power to determine what gains visibility and what remains on the margins, with no transparency over their criteria and no mechanism for accountability. What is clear is that, for these platforms, defending their economic interests and maximizing their profits prevails above user rights, public interest, and democracy itself.

articles.title: Justice, accountability, more questions: what Russell Brand’s guilty verdict means for victim-survivors
articles.author: Anastasia Powell, Professor of Family and Sexual Violence, RMIT University
paras: British comedian and actor Russell Brand has been found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, related to multiple victims, after a four-week trial in London.
He was acquitted on three other charges.
The offences for which Brand was convicted occurred nearly two decades ago.
Meanwhile, United Kingdom police are investigating further allegations of rape made by two other women.
For the six women who came forward to report their experiences, the verdict marks the culmination of a long and undoubtedly difficult journey through the criminal legal system.
Much of the public attention will now likely turn to Brand himself: his sentence, his public reputation and whether he will seek to appeal.
But we should also be asking what this verdict means for victim-survivors of sexual violence.
Sexual violence is common but justice is rare

Though the Brand case occurred in the UK, the rates of sexual violence and trends in justice outcomes are very similar there as they are in Australia. Unfortunately, when we examine those trends, we see justice in response to sexual violence is incredibly rare.
In Australia, one in five women has experienced sexual assault since the age of 15. Yet only about 8% report it to police. Of these, very few proceed to court.
Of those who do report, about one in four do so in the first year after the assault. For most, however, it takes several years before reporting to police. Often this is because of:
a feeling police won’t be able to do anything
fearing they won’t be believed
fearing repercussions from the perpetrator.
For the few who do have their day in court, it is widely recognised that legal processes can cause further harm, or a “second violence” which can exacerbate trauma through:
legal processes of repeatedly providing accounts of what occurred
Justice remains rare, yet is it really justice when the legal process is itself so often the source of further harm to victim-survivors?
Consent is active, specific and can be withdrawn any time
One of the wider and more positive implications of the Brand verdict is it reinforces some fundamental principles of sexual consent.

In Australia, and similarly in the UK, consent means active and free agreement. Consent can be given for some acts and not others, and it can be withdrawn at any time – including during an otherwise consensual sexual encounter.
This was a clear takeaway from the Brand conviction.
In one instance, the victim-survivor had initially agreed to sexual activity with him, but described how he subsequently violated her boundaries and continued despite her asking him to stop.
The jury’s verdict affirms a person’s right to determine what sexual activity they want to engage in, and their right to withdraw consent at any time.
Yet, persistent attitudes and “rape myths” surrounding men’s sexual entitlement have long undermined these core principles of consent. Often it is victim-survivors who are blamed.
Celebrity and social power can further reinforce such dynamics, particularly where influential men are surrounded by institutions and peers willing to excuse or minimise harmful behaviour.
Fame and status should never diminish anyone’s right to bodily autonomy.
Perpetrator accountability is vital
For survivors of sexual violence, a guilty verdict can offer a profoundly important form of justice: recognition that a wrong has been committed and the person responsible is held accountable.
Yet we should perhaps be cautious about assuming a criminal conviction, and incarceration of the perpetrator, will always bring closure and healing for survivors.

The consequences of sexual violence can persist long after criminal proceedings conclude. Survivors may continue to experience the emotional, relational and practical impacts of their experiences, including the additional distress associated with pursuing justice.
And it is important to recognise the absence of a guilty verdict does not mean the absence of any harm.
Accountability takes many forms. Some victim-survivors seek criminal accountability of the perpetrator, while others may seek recognition through other means, including restorative justice processes.
Perpetrator accountability can also take the form of apology and a commitment to positive change. Unfortunately, this form of accountability is rarely seen.

Brand’s conviction is arguably a significant moment of accountability and recognition. For many victim-survivors watching, it may offer some reassurance that even powerful men can be held accountable for their use of violence.
But it is important to recognise that one high-profile conviction cannot undo the injustice many survivors experience.

We need justice systems that are more accessible and trauma-responsive, as well as institutions that are willing to confront sexual violence. We need wider community change to ensure sexual violence is taken seriously, and that survivors are not blamed and shamed for another person’s use of harm. And we need greater emphasis on genuine perpetrator accountability, through recognition of harm caused and a commitment to change.
The women involved in this case have been deservedly praised for their courage. It is no small burden they have carried to seek justice.
Ultimately, though, we should be working towards legal systems and a society where survivors do not have to demonstrate extraordinary courage simply to be heard and supported.

The National Sexual Assault, Family and Domestic Violence Counselling Line – 1800 RESPECT (1800 737 732) – is available 24 hours a day, seven days a week for any Australian who has experienced, or is at risk of, family and domestic violence and/or sexual assault.

Anastasia Powell teaches family violence specialist casework in the Graduate Certificate in Domestic & Family Violence at RMIT University. Anastasia receives funding from the Australian Research Council, is a director of Our Watch (Australia's national organisation for the prevention of violence against women), and works in direct practice with survivors of sexual violence. She is the author of the book 'The Aftermath of Trauma' (Palgrave, 2026) and host of the podcast 'Trauma & Transformation'.

articles.title: JD Vance singled out Iran War for midterm rout – he didn’t say what should happen next in conflict
articles.author: Javed Ali, Associate Professor of Practice of Public Policy, University of Michigan
paras: While votes were still being counted in the U.S. midterm elections, administration figures in Washington were already inviting speculation over how the results might be connected to the conflict with Iran.

On the morning after the election, Vice President JD Vance wrote on X that the major reason for the dramatic loss for Republicans was the American public’s opposition to the war. “Everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there,” he wrote, in reference to the ongoing conflict that began with U.S.-Israeli airstrikes against Iran in late February 2026.

While it is rare for a vice president to make such a critical proclamation about their own administration’s policy, President Donald Trump later stated that he did not disagree with Vance’s appraisal of the role that frustration with the Iran war played in voters’ minds.

But whether this changes Trump’s view on next steps in the ongoing conflict remains unclear. Reporting over the past few weeks has indicated that the U.S. military has been actively preparing options and increasing capabilities in the Persian Gulf region in the event the president directs a resumption of hostilities.

As an expert on Middle East affairs and a former senior official at the National Security Council during the first Trump administration, I’m aware that months of conflict have failed to bring Iran to its knees, force regime change or militarily defeat a perceived threat to U.S. assets and allies. Escalating now is unlikely to change those realities – and it carries the additional risk of further damaging Republicans in the eyes of Americans voters as they turn toward the 2028 presidential race.
Even if Trump were to ratchet up the conflict, moreover, it’s unclear how much wiggle room he’ll have come January facing a Democratic Congress almost uniformly opposed to the war.

Part of the issue facing Iran war hawks in Washington now is that the conflict has caused serious setbacks for the regime in Tehran without satisfying the officially stated strategic reasons for going to war.

They argue that pulling back now – as welcome as that might be for Americans struggling with the associated rising cost of fuel – may allow Iran to rebuild before the conflict is “won.” Moreover, it would render the military and reputational costs already sunk by Washington as wasted.

Among the achievements of this war touted by the Trump administration has been the death of former Supreme Leader Ali Khameini, along with the killing of scores of senior leaders within the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps – including individuals like the former head of Iran’s National Security Council Ali Larijani. Significant elements of Iran’s air defense and radar network, ballistic missile and drone production, and storage and launch sites have also been destroyed. And Iran’s already outdated navy and air force has been further degraded.

Meanwhile, the U.S.-imposed naval blockade against Iranian-linked shipping in the Persian Gulf cut off a crucial lifeline for Iran’s economy. And additional sanctions and economic penalties imposed by Washington have served to further devalue Iran’s currency and deprive Iran of additional financial links to the international banking system.

Yet for all the U.S. successes in degrading the Iranian military by limitless aerial bombardment and the significant financial pressure against the Iranian economy, an obvious endgame remains elusive.

Despite weakening the Iranian government – now led by Ali Khameinei’s son, Mojtaba, and a new echelon of senior IRGC commanders – the Islamic Republic remains intact. Moreover, it still possesses enough ballistic missiles and drones to hold the region at risk, while continuing to impose significant control over its population.

Meanwhile, U.S. military spending continues to rise. In September, the U.S. Congressional Budget Office assessed that the military costs of the Iran War had already totaled US$38 billion. Since then, that number has only increased. And that is to say nothing of the associated global economic costs that have resulted from Iran’s de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz – a key shipping route for oil and gas.

Should Trump decide to change course on Iran, he – and others – may think that the money, effort and lives of 19 American servicemen killed in the conflict would have been spent with no obvious objective achieved. Yet continued military expenditure with no strategic endgame could only magnify those same costs.

To Iran, the midterm results have not changed its public position. Mojtaba Khameini has issued statements directing the IRGC to widen the conflict in the region and perhaps beyond should the U.S. and Israel attack again. At the same time, a statement attributed to him indicates that hostilities between the United States and Iran will persist regardless of the balance of party political power in Washington.

This raises questions about the prospects for diplomacy. During the summer, the U.S. and Iran agreed to an initial 14-point memorandum of understanding that, if finalized, could have brought a permanent end to the hostilities. But since the 60-day clock on that agreement lapsed, no parallel diplomatic agreement has emerged.

Even with the major shift in the U.S. political landscape, it remains unclear whether Trump will resume operations against Iran before the new Congress is sworn in. The messy election result in Israel – which has left the pro-war, and potentially outgoing, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyanu with potentially more reason to double-down in Iran – only complicates matters.

The U.S. military certainly appears to be ready to engage in a new round of attacks against Iran if so directed, and Iran is ready to retaliate. But given the shortcomings in the U.S. inventory – with munitions and missile and air defense capabilities depleted by eight months of war – escalation is something Trump and his inner circle will have to consider with caution.

Iran might force the issue by engaging in asymmetric attacks in the region or beyond that they have not attempted already. Or it could launch a coordinated offensive with its partners in the region – notably the Houthis in Yemen, who have become more active in their own conflict with Saudi Arabia in recent months.
But save an event that the Trump administration perceives is giving it cover to act, there are no clear indications emerging from Washington as to which way it will move.

Vance diagnosed a widely perceived political problem for Republicans: Voters don’t want more war. But what he noticeably didn’t mention was a practical solution. The Middle East conflict – and the United States’ role in it – are, as such, locked in a stalemate.
America and Iran have both borne significant political, military and economic costs. A decision not to pursue an endgame would leave those sunk; doing so may only increase them.

articles.title: Born in Aussie or NZ, playing for the Pacific: the startling demographics of the Rugby League World Cup
articles.author: Jesse Whitehead, Senior Research Fellow,  Te Ngira Institute for Population Research, University of Waikato
paras: The Rugby League World Cup (RLWC) reaches its semi-finals this weekend, in a tournament that’s been marked by upsets, nail-biting finishes and some lopsided scorelines.

On Saturday in Newcastle, New Zealand’s Kiwi Ferns face Fetu Samoa in the women’s competition, before the Kiwis take on an unbeaten Tonga. Sunday’s matches in Sydney see Australia’s Jillaroos meet Fiji, while their counterparts the Kangaroos face Samoa in a rematch of the previous RLWC men’s final.
Pacific nations feature in all four semi-finals. But while the teams represent countries across the region, the vast majority of their players were born in Australia or New Zealand.
Our analysis of the semi-final squads found 85% of the women and 95% of the men were born in these two countries. Many have also represented other nations during their international careers.
These figures speak to the tight connections between Pacific countries, Australia and New Zealand – and the opportunities rugby league offers players with ties to more than one nation.
Small populations, big ties
By comparing squad profiles with population data, we can see how migration, family connections and population trends are reflected on the rugby league field.

Population size is no guarantee of success in international rugby league. England and France, with populations of around 59 million and 66 million respectively, have already been eliminated. Yet Tonga, home to just 105,000 people, has reached the men’s semi-finals.

The Cook Islands, with fewer than 15,000 residents, is the smallest country represented at the tournament. Although the Cook Islands is not in the semi-finals, seven players across the remaining squads have previously represented this proud nation, including Kiwi stars Charnze Nicoll-Klokstad and Apii Nicholls.
Generations of migration across Te Moana Nui a Kiwa (the Pacific Ocean) and the Tasman Sea have created deep family ties between these countries.

In the women’s semi-finals, 57% of players were born in Australia and another 28% in New Zealand. Twelve players across the Kiwi Ferns and Samoa squads have previously represented other countries, highlighting the overlapping national ties within Pacific rugby league.

The Australia-Fiji semi-final, meanwhile, presents a different picture. Only one Jillaroos player in the final team list, Tiana Penitani Gray, has previously represented another country (Tonga), while none of Fiji’s players have done so.

Club affiliations show a similar concentration in Australia: 86% of players across the four women’s semi-final squads compete in the National Rugby League Women’s Premiership (NRLW). They are based mostly with Australian clubs, though seven play with New Zealand’s Warriors Women. Fiji is the only team to draw heavily on players from outside the competition.

In the men’s semi-finals, 95% of players were born in Australia (50%) or New Zealand (45%). Seventeen players in the NZ-Tonga squads have previously represented another country, while just two players across the four men’s semi-final teams compete outside the National Rugby League (NRL).
The strong presence of NRL and NRLW players also highlights the sporting opportunities available in Australia and New Zealand, and the increasingly diverse populations of both countries.
We see such trends in wider migration patterns. In 2023, Australia and New Zealand recorded net migration gains, while Tonga, Samoa and Fiji experienced net losses.

Another notable demographic trend is the relatively young populations of Pacific nations. As governments around the world prepare for ageing populations and growing demand for services and pensions, the Pacific remains comparatively youthful.
That’s interestingly mirrored in the World Cup squads.

In the women’s competition, New Zealand (median age 27 years) and Australia (26) have considerably older squads than Fiji and Samoa (both 22). The pattern is similar among the men, with New Zealand (29) and Australia (28) fielding older squads than Samoa (26) and Tonga (24).

The differences are even more pronounced in the wider populations. The median ages of New Zealanders (37) and Australians (38) are much higher than those of people in Fiji (28), Tonga (21) and Samoa (20).
Within New Zealand, we can point to a similar pattern. The median age of NZ Europeans is 42, compared with 29 for Fijian New Zealanders, 24 for Samoan New Zealanders and 22 for Tongan New Zealanders.
These younger populations offer what we call a “demographic dividend”: the potential economic benefits as a growing share of the population enters its working and income-earning years.
But these benefits aren’t automatic. Realising them requires investment in young people’s health, education and skills, as well as opportunities to develop their talents and aspirations.
When talent meets opportunity

Many players representing Pacific nations in this weekend’s semi-finals grew up a long way from the islands they now represent. They and their families were drawn to Australia and New Zealand by opportunities in education, employment and sport.

Yet when the chance came, many chose to wear the jersey that reflects their identity, family ties and culture. Their achievements show what’s possible when young people have opportunities to develop their talents.
Building on that momentum means continuing to invest in young people, on and off the field, so the next generation can thrive – wherever they call home.

articles.title: What comes after networked authoritarianism?
articles.author: Rebecca MacKinnon
paras: October’s Spotlight contributors illuminated a range of political, economic, and geographic contexts
Originally published on Global Voices
Image by Gerd Altmann on Pixabay.

Fifteen years ago I wrote an article about “networked authoritarianism,” describing China as “exhibit A” for how an authoritarian state adapts to the internet and then adapts digital technologies to increase its own power. I sought to counter prevailing narratives of the time that the internet and tech companies were intrinsically a liberating, democratizing force. While such narratives were eventually discredited, we must not give up on our ability to use technology to defend and exercise our rights. Nor can we simply demand that governments and companies solve the problems they jointly continue to create.

October’s spotlight on Big Tech and Authoritarianism explored a range of relationships between tech companies and political actors across the global majority. Power is wielded through digital technologies in many ways. There are no quick fixes or easy solutions to stop abuses.

But we are not helpless: our Global Voices community has a role to play in strengthening solidarity and cooperation among people fighting to defend their rights, hold abusers accountable, and claim agency over our information environments.

Spotlight contributors illuminated a range of political, economic, and geographic contexts: from Brazil to Hong Kong, Kenya, Myanmar, Palestine, Venezuela, Xinjiang and beyond. They’ve told stories of how different types of governments (or sometimes political insurgents) leverage geopolitical alliances, relationships with tech companies, regulatory power, or other advantages in order to expand political or military dominance, manipulate public opinion, or exercise direct control over citizens. Meanwhile, companies use their own technologies, resources, and government relationships to expand market access and profit.

Tech power is often wielded in ways that make it harder for ordinary people to fight back against abuses. In some cases it is difficult, if not impossible, to prove who has committed what abuse and whether it was intentional — even while harm to individuals or communities has clearly occurred. In other cases, companies discover abuse of their systems to threaten, silence, surveil, or mislead users only after the damage has been done. In Brazil, one expert warns of “governance washing.” An NGO leader working in West Asia and North Africa warns of the rise of a cottage industry of organizations focused on tech accountability without measurably preventing harms.
The dangers of regulation without accountability and public oversight

In North America and Europe, government regulation of Big Tech is often touted as a silver bullet for protecting citizens from harm. But stories from Bangladesh, Kenya and the DRC illustrate different ways that without rigorous safeguards, regulation and enforcement in the name of holding Big Tech accountable can be abused by governments to threaten, track, or discredit critics and political rivals.

Our contributors pointed to conditions that must be met if we are to prevent government abuse of regulations. Laws and regulations need to be evaluated for their compatibility with human rights standards, and reformed or rejected if they fall short. Citizens — through the free press, watchdog NGOs, whistleblower protections and grievance mechanisms — need to be able to monitor and document harms and abuses with clear process for redress and remedy. Sadly, most democracies fail to hold governments — let alone companies — accountable for protecting human rights.

Then there is the even harder problem of what multinational companies should do after a coup or military takeover, leaving users’ data exposed with deadly consequences. Such cases underscore the vital importance of encryption, data security training for civil society, and corporate data minimization practices.
Rejecting techno-imperialism and great power competition

A number of stories describe how global powers leverage their national tech companies to advance strategic and economic interests well beyond their own borders. The companies in turn benefit from such relationships to expand their own global market access, serving as opaque information intermediaries and channels of digital infrastructure.

There has been much media reporting on China’s global tech strategy as a form of its growing soft power. (At the same time, at least one Chinese company insists it is operating independently and should not be treated as an agent of its home government.) But China is not acting alone: It is actually part of a network of authoritarian states, including Russia, Iran, and North Korea, building an international market for digital surveillance. Customers include many countries often described as democracies.

This eye-opening piece points out that, before the U.S. removal of Venezuelan strongman Nicolás Maduro, then vice president and now interim president Delcy Rodrígues negotiated a deal with the Chinese company iFlytek to jointly develop artificial intelligence. That company has been under U.S. sanctions since 2019, but Australian researchers identified layers of Chinese technology deployed across Venezuela. A UN fact finding mission confirmed that they remain in use despite the interim government’s close relationship with the current U.S. presidential administration.

Meanwhile, this article delves into the consequences of global market competition between the U.S. and China. While highly subsidized Chinese ICT infrastructure brings extra benefits to governments that fear their own people, in many cases Chinese tech is the only affordable option. U.S. reciprocal trade agreements that compel countries to restrict purchases of non-U.S. approved infrastructure may make it harder for signatory countries to bridge their own digital divides — which is another way of disempowering their own citizens by keeping digital services out of reach. The piece raises important questions about how countries can assert digital sovereignty to control their own digital infrastructure.
A call for global solidarity

The Chinese government exercises techno-imperialism against its own citizens. Putin’s regime does the same not only at home but in states the Kremlin views as “near abroad.” The articles in October’s spotlight cover events and harms in the global majority. But as I write from San Francisco on the day after U.S. midterm elections, the people of the U.S. are waking up to how the current occupant of the White House and his allies in Silicon Valley have been practicing techno-imperialism on them.

Tech billionaires and trillionaires have been given free rein to maximize profits at the expense of many Americans’ rights and livelihoods, while hyperscaling the government’s ability to surveil, intimidate and imprison. As this chilling piece from Palestine points out, digital surveillance technologies that are first tested in contexts of military occupation, conquest, and even genocide can be — and are — sold and deployed everywhere that governments can get away with doing so.

Several pieces in the series point to open source, decentralized, and community governed technologies as an antidote to Big Tech, exploitation and weaponization. The challenge lies with finding resources and solid legal footing to build out such technologies and systems — especially when so many governments prefer corporate partners as convenient instruments of control and influence. The good news is that cross-border networks of technologists and grassroots organizations are increasingly collaborating around an alternative vision in which communities have agency over their own information environments.

Networked authoritarianism is a global problem. We will only defeat it with global solidarity. As the African-American voting rights activist Fanny Lou Hamer said in 1971: Nobody’s free until everyone’s free.

articles.title: Unmarried Chinese women are rewriting the marriage script
articles.author: Lina Ma
paras: Chinese women are challenging marriage pressures and redefining what it means to be single.
Originally published on Global Voices
The marriage market at People’s Park in Shanghai, 2013. Photo by Jpbowen via Wikimedia Commons, licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0.

On weekends at Shanghai’s People’s Park, umbrellas covered with handwritten sheets of paper line the paths. Parents stand beside them, exchanging information about their unmarried children: age, height, education, income, and whether they own an apartment. It is one of China’s most famous marriage markets — a place where private hopes and social expectations meet in public since 2005.
For years, the word shengnü (剩女), literally translated as “leftover women,” hovered over many of the women whose profiles appeared there.

The translation sounds strange in English because the original Chinese carries a sharper meaning. The character sheng (剩) does not simply mean “remaining.” It suggests something left behind, something unused. In everyday contexts, it can describe leftover food — something that has passed its ideal moment and may eventually be discarded.

When the term became popular in China in the late 2000s, it was used to describe unmarried urban women, often highly educated professionals, who were considered “too old” for marriage after their late twenties. The label was not just a description of marital status. It turned a personal choice into a social judgment.

But today, if you search Chinese media, the phrase shengnü appears far less frequently than it once did. Instead, a more neutral term, zhonggnü (中女), literally translated as “middle or in-and-between women,” is now more often used to describe unmarried women in their thirties in both mainstream media and social platforms.

While the word has faded, many of the expectations behind it remain. The language around unmarried women has become more circumspect, though still pointed. Instead of openly calling women “leftover,” conversations often appear in softer forms: concerns about women being “too picky,” warnings about missing the “best age” for marriage and childbirth, or questions about why a successful woman still has not found a partner.

Instead of using the neutral term zhonggnü, which still highlights women’s age, some women have created new terms and spaces on social media platforms, such as Xiaohongshu and Douban, to discuss these pressures on their own terms. For example, they have reframed the marriage debate to cuīhūn (催婚) — the repeated pressure from family members to marry — and kǒnghūn (恐婚) — the fear or hesitation surrounding marriage itself.
These words reveal a shift. The conversation is no longer only about why women are failing to meet expectations. Increasingly, women are asking whether those expectations should be followed at all.

On Xiaohongshu, a user writing under the name “十元尼美” (Ten Yuan Nimei) described seven years of pressure to marry, beginning when she graduated from university. By 30, she wrote, the pressure had eased — not because her family had accepted her choices, but because people arranging introductions considered her too old for the matchmaking market. At 34, she said, her parents had almost stopped asking.

Her advice to other women began with creating physical distance. Moving from her home province of Hunan to Beijing had largely confined her parents’ pressure to phone calls; later, she moved to Spain. “Sometimes, freedom comes not from persuasion, but from distance,” she wrote.

Other posts question the pressure itself. One shared by the account “渭北春天树” carried the title —“Pressuring someone to marry is, at its core, a form of expulsion.” (催婚的本质是一种驱逐) These conversations no longer see shengnü or unmarried women as a problem, but are turning the conversation on its head to scrutinize traditional conservative family values.

Some women have even embraced and reclaimed the characterization of shengnü as a form of empowerment. Online, some social media posts explicitly recast the label through a play on Chinese characters: 剩, meaning “leftover,” becomes 胜, meaning “victorious,” with the same pronunciation, shèng. A Xiaohongshu post shared by an account named “Kevin” declares: “I’m not a ‘leftover woman’; I’m a ‘victorious woman.’” It advocates remaining single rather than settling, pursuing personal growth, and enjoying time alone.

In another post, the creator “小李存钱记” addresses her mother’s worries about her being unmarried at 30. “I’m not a leftover woman! I’m a victorious woman!” reads the text across the image. She describes juggling several jobs and building an online following, presenting her work and earnings as evidence of her worth. The reframing rejects marriage as the measure of success, while placing considerable emphasis on professional achievement and financial independence.

These posts do not erase the social stigma of the term shengnü. Rather, they show how users are challenging the label by questioning family pressure, sharing ways to escape it, or replacing “leftover” with “victorious.” Yet the language of victory raises another question. If an unmarried woman must point to her earnings, career, or independence to defend her choices, how much room is there simply to be single?

articles.title: Why AI cannot ‘think’ like humans do
articles.author: Didier Camilo Olarte Gonzalez, PhD Student in Experimental Psychology, Université du Québec à Montréal (UQAM)
paras: Today’s artificial intelligence technologies have become remarkably good at generating text and ideas that seem profoundly human. Chatbots powered by large language models such as ChatGPT, Claude, Google Gemini and Perplexity AI can write poems, brainstorm and find solutions to complex problems.

The developers of these products drew heavily on the human brain for inspiration, creating artificial neural networks based on the workings of human neurons. Their systems now produce outputs that often resemble the outputs of human thinking.
AI and the human mind, however, do not work the same way. Similar results do not necessarily mean similar processes.

“World models” are an emerging technology that could help AI systems move closer to human “thinking” by helping them learn to anticipate what might happen and use that prediction to act. Still, AI will not perceive, learn or understand the world as humanity does.
A falling cup, a complex prediction
Imagine reaching for a cup at the edge of a counter. The cup may fall and smash if you misjudge the distance, grip it too loosely or move too quickly.

For humans, grabbing a cup like this is routine. Yet this simple action relies on the complex ability to anticipate what might happen next. Our minds constantly try to stay one step ahead by understanding events and their causes. We can foresee the mess that would result from moving an overfilled cup or imagine a sofa getting stuck in a doorway even before we buy it.
These predictions draw on expectations that form when we interact with the world. What we anticipate can, in turn, impact how we perceive the world and how we act.

One influential family of theories, known as predictive processing, proposes that perception works partly in this way. The brain generates expectations, compares them to the information it receives and makes adjustments when the two don’t match.

Let’s return to the example of the cup. Imagine reaching for an empty cup that you believe to be full. Your hand, expecting a heavier object, lifts it with more force than necessary. The cup rises abruptly and feels almost weightless. That mismatch provides feedback that helps correct the movement and update your estimate of its weight.
What we anticipate shapes our actions, and what happens next updates our expectations. All this happens just to pick up a cup.
Does AI predict differently?

Even for today’s robots, reliably manipulating cups can require extensive training and simulation. The challenge involves learning how the physical world behaves and predicting the consequences of an action.

Chatbots using large language models also make predictions, but of a different kind. They learn to predict the next word or fragment of text. This apparently simple way of predicting can nevertheless produce remarkably capable systems able to solve complex problems.

Take the sentence: “A hand bumps a cup near the edge of a table. The cup…” Having learned patterns from enormous amounts of data, a chatbot might continue with “tips over the edge and falls to the floor.” It can do so by predicting patterns from a dataset and without ever physically handling a cup.
However, being able to describe plausible outcomes does not necessarily mean a chatbot has learned why they happen.
Teaching a robot to anticipate

This is where world models kick in — a broad family of AI approaches that aim to predict how situations evolve and, in some cases, how actions may change them. These models can learn from videos, simulations or recordings of what robots see and do.
For a domestic robot, this could mean anticipating that gripping too tightly might break the cup, or that a wrong movement could tip it over.
By incorporating actions, motion and sensory information, preliminary research shows these systems can help connect predictions with what happens in the physical world.

A world model could eventually make the same predictions we do about a cup. And as it learns from actions and sensory feedback, the resemblance to us may become increasingly hard to ignore. Still, arriving at the same prediction does not tell us what knowledge supports it or how that knowledge was acquired.
Same prediction, same cognition?

To us, a cup is not only a cylinder on a table. It can be graspable, breakable, yours, mine, too hot or almost falling. Our understanding connects the cup’s physical properties to a network of possible actions and consequences.
Predicting that the cup will fall reveals only a small part of that understanding.

And this understanding develops quite early. Studies suggest that infants just a few months old already have basic expectations about how physical objects behave. Child-development researcher Jean Piaget proposed that children build knowledge through acting on the world. As this knowledge develops, they become able to mentally anticipate consequences without having to carry out each action.

For humans, learning involves more than accumulating information about cups. It involves connecting experiences when reaching for one, feeling its weight, seeing it spill and eventually imagining what might happen without even having to try it.

Using world models, AI can also learn from actions and sensory feedback, in addition to videos, simulations and other data. Like humans, they can learn to interact with the world. The question is how their experiences contribute to the knowledge they build and use.
AI could definitely come closer to anticipating what might happen and using that prediction to act. This alone, however, does not show that AI perceives, learns or understands the world as we do.
As AI gets better at replicating the results of human cognition, distinguishing performance from process will only become more important.
